title: We fight every year about whose family to spend the holidays with
summary: The fight about whose family to visit for the holidays is rarely about logistics. Here's the loyalty question underneath, and how to stop repeating it.
body_markdown:
It starts earlier every year. Someone's mom sends a text about Thanksgiving in October, and suddenly the two of you are having[the same argument](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) you had last December, and the December before that. Whose family. Which holiday. Who gets shortchanged this time. By the time the actual day arrives you are both exhausted before you have even packed a bag.


If this is a yearly ritual in your house, you are not doing the holidays wrong. You are stuck on a question that logistics can't answer, because the fight was never really about the calendar.


## Why the calendar isn't the real problem


On the surface it looks like a scheduling puzzle. Two families, a finite number of days, some math about driving distance. If that were all it was, you would have solved it years ago, the way you solve every other calendar conflict.


What makes it stick is what sits underneath the scheduling. When your partner pushes hard for their family, the thing you actually hear is rarely "I miss my mom." It is closer to "you are choosing them over me." When you push for yours, they hear the exact same thing. Under whose-family-for-the-holidays is a much older question: when the family you came from and the family you are building want different things, who do you put first?


## The loyalty bind nobody says out loud


Here is the pattern we see over and over in Maia conversations. Both people feel like the one being asked to give something up. One partner feels guilty disappointing a parent who is getting older, who "only asks for this one day a year." The other feels quietly unchosen, like they married someone whose real allegiance still lives at their childhood address. Both of those feelings are real. And neither person has said the actual sentence out loud, so instead they argue about drive times and who hosted last year.


You cannot negotiate your way out of a fight when the thing that hurts is never on the table.


## Is it a logistics disagreement or a loyalty one?


It helps to work out which one you are really having, because they need very different things.


- **A logistics disagreement** is solvable with a plan. Alternate years, split the day, one family for Thanksgiving and the other for Christmas. If a fair plan makes most of the tension go away, it was logistics all along.
- **A loyalty disagreement** survives the plan. You can agree to alternate years and still feel, on your off year, like you got overruled, or like[your partner did not defend you when their mom pushed back](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-husband-takes-his-moms-side) . That is the tell: the schedule is fair on paper and someone still feels unchosen. A calendar does not fix this one. Knowing your partner has you, out loud, even when their parent is disappointed, is what fixes it.


## What actually breaks the yearly cycle


The couples who stop having this fight tend to do a few specific things.


**They decide together before either family asks.** The second a parent's invitation lands first, you are negotiating from defense, and whoever's family called dibs "wins." Have the conversation in early November, on your own couch, before anyone's mother has a plan you are reacting to.


**They say the real sentence.** Not "your family always gets Christmas" but the thing underneath it: "I'm scared my mom will feel abandoned," or "I need to know you'll take my side when your dad lays on the guilt." The argument cannot resolve while the actual fear stays hidden behind logistics.


**They go to the families as a team.** Decide as a couple first, then deliver it together.[Setting a boundary with a parent](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/boundaries-the-secret-to-a-stronger-relationship) lands very differently when it comes from both of you rather than from the in-law they can cast as the villain. Your partner handles their family, you handle yours, and neither of you throws the other under the bus to[keep the peace in the moment](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/pretending-everything-is-fine-in-front-of-family) .


**They make a rule once instead of a decision twelve times.** "Odd years your family, even years mine," or "Thanksgiving with them, Christmas with us." A standing plan means next October is not a fresh negotiation. It is just what you do now.


**They protect something of their own.** A slow morning at home before the drive. One small tradition that belongs to neither family. Part of why this fight cuts is that the holidays can start to feel like they belong to everyone except the two of you.


## The moves that keep you stuck


A few things reliably turn a hard conversation into the yearly blowup:


- Letting a parent hear the decision before your partner does. Your partner is the first call, always.
- Keeping score out loud ("we ALWAYS do your family"). Even when the count is accurate, it turns your partner into an opponent instead of a teammate.
- Putting it off. If you keep[avoiding the conversation until it's a crisis](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-avoid-hard-conversations) , you will end up making the whole decision in a fight three days before, when everyone is already tense and half-packed.


If you and your partner run this loop every year, it can help to slow it down somewhere calmer than the week before Thanksgiving. Talking it through with Maia can help you find the sentence underneath the scheduling: what you are each actually afraid of, and what a plan would need to include for both of you to feel chosen. Sometimes naming that once, in a quiet moment, is what finally ends the yearly version of the argument.
